title: Xi’s Gang of Three
gist: Deng Yuwen argues Xi Jinping runs China through a 'gang of three' with Premier Li Qiang (state) and Cai Qi (party), and that Li is likelier than Cai to keep his Standing Committee seat at the 2027 Party Congress because governing a struggling economy needs his skills. Rumors of Li or Cai as designated successor are dismissed as not credible.

insights.claim: Rumors that Premier Li Qiang or Cai Qi has been designated Xi Jinping's successor are not credible, but they reveal that Xi depends on both men to sustain his rule.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Treat succession-rumor headlines about China's leadership as noise; the signal is the division of labor beneath Xi.

insights.claim: Chinese elite politics is best read as a 'central gang of three' framework: Xi at the center, with Li overseeing government affairs and Cai overseeing party affairs, unequal in rank and potential competitors.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Use relationship-mapping rather than photo-and-meeting tea-leaf reading to judge Chinese policy direction.

insights.claim: Unlike Lin Biao and Jiang Qing under Mao, Li and Cai owe their rise solely to Xi's trust and hold no independent political capital, so their interests are more closely aligned with Xi's and neither can build a power center outside his authority.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Lowers the odds of an elite rupture in Beijing in the near term.

insights.claim: Outside observers have repeatedly misjudged Xi's rule by imagining Zhongnanhai as perpetually on the verge of a palace coup while ignoring how the system functions day to day.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Discount palace-coup narratives when sizing China political risk.

insights.claim: Cai Qi ranks fifth in the party hierarchy yet runs the Secretariat's daily work, heads the CCP Central Committee General Office, and this year took charge of the Central Party School, keeping him almost constantly at Xi's side.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Cai is the gatekeeper of information and schedule reaching Xi.

insights.claim: Xi deliberately prevents Cai from monopolizing party affairs: discipline, personnel, propaganda, political-legal and security portfolios sit with other loyalists reporting directly to Xi, and Shi Taifeng was moved to head the Organization Department last year.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Signals Xi guards against any lieutenant turning the party apparatus into a personal base.
insights.locator: 'Moreover, last year Xi transferred Shi Taifeng'

insights.claim: Xi decides how far anti-corruption campaigns go and what ideological campaigns the party runs; Cai only translates Xi's will into daily party-center operations.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Policy intensity on discipline campaigns is a Xi decision, not a Cai one.

insights.claim: Xi has pulled major economic decisions into party bodies such as the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission and Central Financial Commission and given vice premiers Ding Xuexiang and He Lifeng big portfolios, dispersing the premier's authority.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Premier-level statements are only part of China's economic decision chain.
insights.locator: 'Li, of course, operates under numerous constraints'

insights.claim: Because the State Council has its own administrative system and legal powers, and Xi cannot run the government daily, Li retains discretion over day-to-day economic policy within Xi's framework.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Watch State Council implementation for real policy detail.

insights.claim: Facing a lingering real estate crisis, local government debt, weak domestic demand and US strategic pressure, Xi needs a politically reliable premier who can get things done, which is why economic management may matter no less than political rectification.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: China's growth backdrop keeps pressure on the leadership to value governing competence.
insights.locator: 'With China confronting a lingering real estate crisis'

insights.claim: By October 2027 both Li and Cai will be past the customary retirement age of 68, Li by about three months and Cai by nearly four years, so the informal 'seven up, eight down' convention would normally retire both.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Standing Committee turnover at the 21st Party Congress is a key 2027 event to track.

insights.claim: Keeping both men on the Standing Committee appears unlikely because Xi must make room for other loyalists; the author expects Li to have the stronger chance of staying, with Cai possibly retiring only partially, for example staying at the Central Party School or becoming state vice president.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Positions Li as the more durable figure for China economic policy continuity.
insights.locator: 'Keeping both men on the Standing Committee'

insights.claim: The deciding question for Xi is whether he needs an aide who helps him govern the country or one who helps him control the party; as governing grows more complex, dependence on Li may deepen.
insights.speaker: Deng Yuwen
insights.so_what: Governance capacity may outweigh pure loyalty over time.
